newsitem.title: USA: Compaq to unveil PC/TV hybrid system.
newsitem.headline: Compaq to unveil PC/TV hybrid system.

text.p: Compaq Computer Corp. will unveil Monday its entry into the newest home entertainment market -- a powerful PC combined with a big-screen TV.
Compaq's "PC Theater" will compete with Gateway 2000 Inc. "Destination" system in the consumer electronics arena aiming at buyers that Compaq calls "digital upscale believers."
Compaq's home PC Theater system was co-developed with Thomson Consumer Electronics, which owns RCA, and will retail at $4,999, analysts said.
A Compaq spokeswoman in Houston declined to comment.

"This is an entry into some new territory and this is stage one," said Richard Zwetchkenbaum, director of global new media consumer research at International Data Corp. "They want to get out of the office and into the living room."

The PC Theater is a hybrid PC/TV that has a 36-inch screen, a wireless keyboard and a remote control for the PC and TV functions. It can connect to a cable box, a digital satellite programming device, VCR, laser disc player and a digital video disc player.

Consumers will be able to watch TV while simultaneously searching the Internet, play interactive PC games, send electronic mail, or watch films recorded with a video camera on a big television screen with surround-sound speakers.

"It will target the audio-videophile segment of the population," said Van Baker, a Dataquest Inc. analyst. "It's going to be a market that will be slow to develop. We are in the very, very early stages of convergence."

Gateway's Destination system, which was introduced one year ago, has not been a huge revenue-generator, analysts said, but the company made some inroads by creating a stir amid a new group of consumers with the Destination.
Th system started selling at $4,500 when it was launched a year ago this month, but it has now dropped in price to just under $3,000.

"We are very pleased that Compaq is entering the market," said Luanne Flikkema, director of global research at Gateway 2000 in North Sioux City, S.D. "As more companies come into the category, it will enhance the market."

Compaq and Gateway are both targeting upscale, highly-educated, generally younger consumers with children who are not necessarily nerds but who understand the importance of technology. Analysts estimate this market at about 10 million to 15 million households.

"They are not selling a lot, it's not material," said Louis Mazzucchelli, an analyst at Gerard Klauer Mattison, referring to Gateway. But he added that both Gateway and Compaq are not looking to sell a lot of these combined PC/TVs.
"They want to educate the market about machines with the Compaq brand in rooms other than the office," he added.

Gateway said that currently the biggest buyers of the Destination are big families who already own a PC or the corporate education and training market, which combines the computing functions and the big screen for corporate training.
"The majority of people are buying it as a second or a third PC, but the ones who are buying it as a first PC are telling us about its great value," said Flikkema.
Analysts said that Compaq was not looking to sell millions of units of the PC Theater, just hoping to gradually make a name for itself in the home/consumer electronics area.

"Gateway has gotten a lot of mileage out of it (the Destination). It's market presence, not revenues," said IDC's Zwetchkenbaum. "It's not how many units you sell, this is the future. This is what people are going to be doing."

Compaq's new PC Theater has incredible resolution and picture quality that is almost on par with digital television, and analysts said these hybrid PC/TV products may serve as interim solutions for the so-called "early adopters," who are waiting for digital television to arrive late in 1998.
"When this accelerates, it will be after the introduction of digital television," said Dataquest's Baker. "It will be a big stimulus in the convergence space."
